newsitem.title: CHINA: S. Korea offers 50,000 tonnes food aid to North.
newsitem.headline: S. Korea offers 50,000 tonnes food aid to North.

text.p: The South Korean Red Cross offered a further 50,000 tonnes of food aid to North Korea during talks in Beijing on Wednesday, but the northern side said the amount was insufficient, officials said.

Speaking after a first round of talks in the morning, Choe Gyongrin, head of the North Korean Red Cross delegation, said the southern side had offered 50,000 tonnes of grain as food aid to the North, which is on the brink of starvation.
However, Pyongyang had responded by saying that this was not enough, especially when compared with the size of aid donations from other countries, Choe told reporters after the morning talks.
The talks had focused on a range of proposals and various problems and were likely to resume on Thursday, Choe said as he emerged from the meeting. He refused to give further details.
"Today's talks were very friendly and I am very optimistic about the prospects of tomorrow's talks," Choe said.
In Seoul, a South Korean Red Cross official said the 50,000 tonnes of food would be available for delivery by the end of October.

The negotiations follow meetings in Beijing last May when the South Korean Red Cross pledged a similar 50,000 tonnes of grain aid for the Stalinist North. That shipment is due to be completed later this month.
South Korean officials said this round of talks could last for several days.

The previous discussions, the first between the two sides for nearly five years, focused in part on delivery of the aid, with the South insisting the grain be clearly labelled as coming from South Korea.
The South also demanded guarantees the food aid would not be diverted into the hands of Pyongyang's military.

International aid workers say the communist North is on the brink of famine after floods in 1995 and 1996 devastated much of the country's farmland and industrial bases, exacerbating already severe food shortages in the hermit nation.

The latest discussions were agreed to earlier this month when an offer by the South to hold talks for further food aid on the Korean peninsula was met with a counter-proposal by the northern Red Cross to hold the meeting in Beijing.
The Red Cross is the only legal channel for private aid from South Korea to the North.
The aid agreed last May came on top of $16 million worth of donations made by Seoul in response to an appeal by the United Nations World Food Programme.
Washington also this month nearly doubled its total food aid to North Korea to $52 million, intended to combat widespread malnutrition, particularly among children.
